storm.summary_layperson: Scattered strong storms are near the region but currently tracking away to the north, and any that reach us won't get the usual cooling boost from crossing the Sound — so the risk here tonight is about the same as inland towns, not reduced.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The tracked cells are approaching from the north-northeast over land, not across the Sound, so the marine layer's storm-weakening effect doesn't apply tonight — moot anyway, since its 9°F buffer fades to about 3°F by 6 PM and is gone by 9 PM as the air cools.
storm.detail_html:
OKX radar shows a cluster of moderate-to-strong cells (up to 52 dBZ) about 30 miles north-northeast of the cove, plus a weaker cluster near the NY/NJ line to the southwest. Both groups are tracking away from Greenwich Cove (measured storm motion near 46 kt toward the WNW), while CAPE is building steadily through the evening — 340 J/kg now, rising toward roughly 1,000–1,200 J/kg by 9–10 PM — alongside 35+ kt of deep-layer shear. That combination supports isolated strong-to-severe cells overnight, consistent with the "marginal severe" wording in this afternoon's NWS Upton (OKX) forecast discussion. A Coastal Flood Statement is in effect later tonight; no severe thunderstorm or tornado watches/warnings are currently posted.

Normally the cool Sound water (74°F vs 82°F air, a 9°F gap) sets up a stabilizing marine layer that can weaken storms crossing it before they reach shore. That mechanism doesn't apply tonight: the tracked cells are approaching from the north-northeast, a path that stays mostly over land and never crosses open Sound water, so there's no cool-water transit to sap their energy. Even if a cell did track over the water, the marine layer itself is fading fast — the 9°F gap right now shrinks to about 3°F by 6 PM and is under 1°F by 9 PM as the air cools after sunset while the Sound holds steady near 74°F.

Net effect for the cove: storm risk here is essentially the same as surrounding inland towns tonight, not reduced the way the waterfront sometimes provides. The good news is the tracked cells are currently moving away rather than closing in; the bigger watch item is any new cell that fires later this evening as CAPE keeps climbing.

What would change the call: a new cell developing to the west or southwest and tracking NE/ENE toward the cove (that path would put Sound-crossing back in play, though tonight's steep NNE motion argues against it); a severe thunderstorm or tornado warning for southern Fairfield/Westchester counties; or an upstream APRS gust spike at the Rye/Port Chester stations signaling an approaching outflow boundary.

wind.tactics_blurb: RYC now: S 183° at 9 kt (10-min avg 5, gusting 9). Pure thermal sea-breeze day with no gradient reinforcement — holds SSW ~205° at 7–9 kt through around 7 PM, then collapses toward light/variable 5 kt or less by 9–10 PM (sea breeze dies ~7:28 PM, about 30 min ahead of the 7:58 PM sunset). Pressure is fairly even across the course with a touch more breeze on the east side; play the oscillations rather than committing hard to one side.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
DeltaT (the air–water temperature difference) is 8.6°F between inland air (82.4°F) and the Sound (73.8°F), clearing the 5°F sea-breeze threshold with room to spare. The pipeline's own sea-breeze proxy flags today as a pure thermal day rather than gradient-reinforced: the background synoptic flow, best read from the inland Westchester station (KHPN, WSW at 4 kt), is light with an offshore component, meaning the wind at the cove right now is essentially all thermal, not a gradient tailwind. RYC currently reads S 183° at 9.1 kt (10-min avg 5.2), gusting 9.4 — a mature, established sea breeze.

HRRR's raw model direction (S 190°) is running about 38° behind the real, more-veered western-LIS sea breeze that stations are already showing (SW 228°); applying the maturation correction puts the trusted near-term forecast direction at SSW 205°, which is what's used for the hourly table above rather than the raw model output.

With SSW flow running up the cove's north–south axis, pressure should stay fairly even across the course, with a touch more breeze on the east side near the mouth where there's less shelter than the west shore's channeling. No side is badly disadvantaged tonight.

The sea breeze has been running long enough this afternoon to be past the first two-hour "ramping" phase, so expect it to oscillate roughly ±10° around the SSW mean through the early part of the window — playable shifts, not a big commit-right day.

Being a pure, non-reinforced thermal day, this sea breeze dies at sunset minus 30–60 minutes: the pipeline's own collapse estimate is 7:28 PM EDT, about 30 minutes ahead of the 7:58 PM sunset. Expect speed to ease from the 7–9 kt range into the 5–6 kt range through 8 PM, then fall further into light/variable 5-kt-or-under conditions by 9–10 PM as a weak background WSW/SW flow takes over.

Racing translation: 7–9 kt through about 7 PM is solid one-design dinghy sailing; by 9–10 PM it drops into the 5-kt-or-under drifter zone where most fleets will struggle to keep steerage. Plan racing for the front half of the window and treat anything after 8:30–9 PM as a bonus, not a given.
